translation: "Shut up," said the optician once again louder and walked faster, "Selma only very rarely finds something threatening or unattractive.
He was completely right about that, but unfortunately he had said more than he should have replied to the voices.
But love she might find particularly unattractive, whispered the voices.
There must be a reason, they said, why the truth has been hidden for so long.
"It was cowardice," said the optician and shifted his leather bag to his other hip because the jostling of the bag and voices began to hurt.
"It was prudence," said the voices, "Fear can sometimes be a good advisor," they suggested humming along with an early evening TV show's theme tune.
The optician started walking slower now.
The path to Selma's house which normally took him ten minutes seemed suddenly like an all-day journey with very heavy baggage indeed.
That was true.
The dog was the color of slushy snow, a washed-out gray and shaggy like a pure Irish Wolfhound without anything else mixed in.
His body was still small, but his paws were as large as bear claws, and we all knew what that meant.
Selma remained standing straight in front of the kitchen bench.
She looked at the dog for a long time.
Then she looked at my father as if he were a gift shop.
Farmer Häubel was firmly convinced that Death would be polite, just as Farmer Häubel himself had been throughout his life.
He was sure that Death wouldn't snatch away his life, but rather gently take it from his hand.
He imagined Death softly knocking on the door, opening it just a crack and asking, "May I?" to which Farmer Häubel would naturally respond affirmatively.
"Of course," Farmer Häubel would say.
"Please come in," and Death would enter.
He'd stand beside Farmer Häubel's bed and ask: "Is this a good time for you? I can always come back later if you'd like.
But Farmer Häubel would sit up straight and say, "No no, now is a very good time for me", adding quickly: "Let's not postpone any longer; who knows when you could manage to come again.
And then death would take a seat on the chair already prepared at the head of the bed.
Apologizing in advance for the coldness of his hands—which wouldn't bother farmer Haübel—he'd gently lay one hand over Haübel's eyes.
The people in the village were troubled; you could see it on their faces, even though most of them tried their best not to show it.
This morning, just a few hours after Selma's dream, people moved about the village as if flash ice had formed on all its paths not just outside but also inside the houses.
Flash ice formed in the kitchens and living rooms.
They moved as if their own bodies felt completely alien to them, as if all their joints were inflamed and even the objects they handled could spontaneously combust.
All day long they regarded life suspiciously—both theirs and others' lives—as far as possible.

They constantly looked behind themselves to check whether someone might spring at them with murderous intent—a person who'd lost their mind and therefore had nothing significant to lose—and quickly switched focus forward again because that same madman could attack from the front too.
They looked up frequently, determined to avoid falling roof tiles or heavy lampshades from overhead.

They avoided all animals because they thought that insanity would emerge faster from animals than from humans—they kept a distance from benign cows who might suddenly kick out today; they avoided dogs—even very old ones that could hardly stand anymore—for fear said dogs might still attack viciously today for no reason whatsoever.
Apart from Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, most of the villagers were not superstitious.

They nonchalantly did all the things one shouldn't do when superstitious: they calmly sat under wall clocks even though superstitions suggest it can lead to death; they slept with their heads facing the door, which in superstition indicates that you will soon be carried out feet first through that very door.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year's, which Elsbeth warned was tantamount to suicide or an accessory to murder according to superstition.
They did not get startled when an owl hooted at night, when a horse in the stable sweated heavily, or when a dog howled at night with its head down.
The train ride lasted fifteen minutes, with no intermediate stops.
Since our first train ride, we always played the same game:
We would stand with our backs to the windows by the opposite train doors.
Martin would close his eyes; I would look out of the door window that Martin had his back to.
In first grade, I told Martin everything I saw during our journey and he tried to memorize everything.

He was very good at it so that in second grade, I didn't have to narrate anything anymore and Martin could recite almost everything that I just saw through the fogged-up train window while standing backward with his eyes closed: "Wire factory," he said at exactly the moment we passed by it.
Then "Field.

Field.
Forest.

Pastureland.

Village.
Pasture.
Field.

"What else could it have been?" said Selma, pointing out that one would hardly mistake an okapi for another animal.
"Well," I said, "it could've been a malformed cow, a wrongly constructed giraffe, a whim of nature the stripes and rust-red color can't be clearly seen at night when everything is blurry.
"That's nonsense," Selma retorted as she rubbed her forehead.
"Unfortunately, that's complete nonsense, Luise.
She placed a slice of cheese on the bread, folded it together and put it in my sandwich box.
"Do you know exactly when you had this dream?"
"Around three o'clock," Selma replied.

She jolted awake after the image of the okapi had receded; sitting upright in bed and staring at her nightgown as she realized she was no longer in her dream standing on Uhlheck then glanced over to the alarm clock: three o'clock.
"We probably shouldn't take it too seriously," said Selma; yet she spoke with the resignation of a TV detective disregarding an anonymous note.
"What's wrong?"
I asked.
"Nothing," trilled Selma, opening the fridge, pulling out a packet of sliced cheese and liver sausage and waving them through the air.
"What would you like on your sandwiches for school?" she trilled.
"Little mouse," she added with another trill; her continued trilling and nicknaming were now really alarming.
"Cheese, please" I said, "what's up with you?"
"Nothing", chirped Selma, repeating what she had just said.
She spread butter on a slice of bread and in her distraction knocked the cheese off the countertop with her wrist while flitting about aimlessly.
Now still at last, Selma stared down at the pack of cheese as if it were something precious that had shattered into a thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamed of an okapi three times in her life, and each time someone had died afterwards, so we were convinced that a dream about an okapi and death were definitely linked.
Our minds work this way.
They can quickly create solid connections between the most unlikely things.
Like coffee pots and shoelaces, for instance, or deposit bottles and fir trees.
When I slept downstairs with Selma, she would tell me stories with happy endings by the bedside.
When I was younger, I always grasped her wrist after the stories, placed my thumb on her pulse, and imagined that the whole world was doing everything in rhythm with Selma's heartbeat.

I envisioned how the optician ground lenses, Martin lifted a weight, Elsbeth trimmed her hedge, how the grocer stocked juice cartons, my mother layered fir twigs on top of each other , my father stamped prescriptions all in sync with Selma's heartbeat.
This always put me reliably to sleep but now at ten years old, Selma thought I was too old for that.
